discussion_points: Which explicit information properties should a user question be able to steer?
Which released human reference can legitimately validate a computational accessibility metric?
How should systems communicate uncertainty and avoid unsupported social or identity inference?
ethics_note: This anonymous review-stage project is a secondary analysis of released research data and frozen model outputs; no new human data were collected. Applicable institutional determination remains required before external dissemination.
sample_summary: Locked design: N = 1000 image-question items × 3 frozen prompt conditions; 2 frozen computational measurement models; released human-reference calibration.

findings: RQ2: task-answer and spatial properties were preselected for the intent-versus-generic contrast; Figure 2 reports frozen computational estimates.
RQ3: human-answer and caption overlap quantify bounded external human-reference alignment, not preference or ratings.
RQ4: Dream/intent and human-caption/AI distances compare text profiles only, not cognition or accessibility value.
RQ5: identity and social-intent inference are model-derived output properties, not measured harms or lived experience.
implications: Accessibility evaluation should test whether steering changes explicit task, spatial, social, identity, and uncertainty information rather than generic visual detail alone.
Dream-language resemblance and human-reference alignment should remain distinct evaluation targets; neither alone establishes lived accessibility value.
limitations: Synthetic labels are computational measurements, not human judgments or substitutes for blind and low-vision lived experience.
Released captions and answers are bounded external references; they do not establish BLV preference, usefulness, safety, or semantic correctness.
DreamSpace comparisons concern textual distributions only. This study does not test dream incorporation, cognition, neural change, or causal effects on people.
Measurement status and model-family disagreement remain in the provenance record; unstable or non-estimable measurements cannot support substantive claims.
methods: Historical blind dream reports, BLV-originating questions, released human references, and a locked within-item VLM intervention were mapped to one sensory-information ontology.
Each locked image-question item was generated under generic, BLV-intent-steered, and accessibility-steered prompts using the same frozen VLM configuration.
Two frozen model-family judges provide computational text measurements; released human-labelled datasets provide external calibration, not same-item human ratings.

subtitle: A controlled within-item VLM intervention compares DreamSpace, BLV-originating intent, released human references, and AI-mediated output while separating model-derived text measurement from human judgment.
title: What Blind People Dream, Ask, and What AI Tells Them: A Public-Data Study of Sensory Mediation in the AI Age
